entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Nancy Cathedral (Cathédrale Notre-Dame-de-l'Annonciation de Nancy) in Lorraine, France, built 1703-1742 CE in the Baroque style — one of France's finest Baroque cathedrals — was the court church of the Duchy of Lorraine and later became famous through its connection to Stanisław Leszczyński, the deposed King of Poland who ruled Lorraine (1737-1766) and transformed Nancy into one of the most beautiful Baroque cities in Europe with his construction of the Place Stanislas (1752-1756).

Nancy's Place Stanislas — built by Stanisław Leszczyński with his architect Emmanuel Héré de Corny — is one of the most complete and beautiful 18th-century royal squares in Europe, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983) and France's most magnificent Baroque ensemble. The cathedral forms part of this broader urban composition: Nancy under Stanisław became a showcase of French Rococo architecture, wrought-iron grillwork (by Jean Lamour), and urban planning that influenced European city design.

Stanisław Leszczyński's story is one of history's more poignant: twice elected King of Poland (1704, 1733), twice deposed, he received Lorraine as a consolation prize from his son-in-law Louis XV after the War of the Polish Succession — and transformed his loss into a cultural triumph by making Nancy one of Europe's most beautiful capitals. The cathedral was damaged during the French Revolution but restored; it remains an active cathedral and part of the UNESCO-protected Nancy Baroque ensemble.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nancy Cathedral — part of the UNESCO-protected Baroque ensemble built by deposed Polish King Stanisław Leszczyński, whose cultural patronage transformed political exile into one of Europe's most beautiful cities — is a monument to 18th-century French Baroque urban achievement.
